# Craft guilds and apprenticeship (`guilds_apprenticeship`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/institutions.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Institutions, law & governance (`institutions`)
- Deps: helped by commercial_law_contract_enforcement, standard_weights_measures
- Core idea: A written apprenticeship contract binds a youth to a master for a fixed term (often five to seven years): the master gives board and teaches the whole craft, the apprentice repays with cheap labour in the later years, and a guild or town registers and enforces the contract. This solves the problem that skill cannot be bought in a shop and that a master will not teach someone who may walk away half-trained. Guilds also set quality marks, inspect goods, and support sick members and widows. Understand them as well because every new device in a guild town has to pass them.
- Pitfalls:
  - Treating guilds as mere obstacles to remove: they are the town's government, militia and welfare system, and they will ruin a stranger who undersells their members
  - Introducing a labour-saving machine without a guild's consent: looms and mills were smashed and inventors expelled (ribbon loom bans from the 16th c.)
  - The opposite error of idealising them: guilds restricted entry, excluded women, Jews and outsiders, and kept prices up
  - Expecting a master to reveal trade secrets to a visitor: knowledge is his property and the guild's
- History: mesopotamia: c. 1754 BC – Hammurabi §§188–189 on craftsmen teaching adopted sons; 6th c. BC Babylonian apprenticeship contracts with fixed terms and penalties; india: from c. 5th c. BC – shreni (guilds) of craftsmen and merchants with headmen, rules and seals, which also took deposits and managed endowments; rome: collegia of craftsmen, mainly social and religious; apprenticeship contracts on papyrus from Roman Egypt (1st–3rd c. AD); china: Tang–Song – trade associations (hang) by street and craft, used by the state for requisitions; native-place guilds (huiguan) from the Ming; islamic: craft organisations in Islamic cities are clear from the 14th–16th c. (earlier existence disputed); europe: early 10th c. – Byzantine Book of the Eparch regulates trades in Constantinople; 11th–12th c. merchant and craft guilds in Italian, Flemish and Rhenish towns; 1563 English Statute of Artificers fixes seven years; abolished in France 1791; africa: craft guilds and hereditary craft groups in Benin (brass casters) and the Hausa cities
- Read:
  - Sheilagh Ogilvie, The European Guilds: An Economic Analysis (2019)
  - S. R. Epstein, Craft Guilds, Apprenticeship, and Technological Change in Preindustrial Europe, Journal of Economic History 58 (1998)
